endorsements.quote: This led to the establishment of a governance group that reflects the important stakeholders and decision-makers in our healthcare system, including consumers and Māori.
The next step was establishing a new AI Governance Group (AIGG) for Te Whatu Ora Waitematā.

The process for approval emphasises the importance of working with a range of end-user and expert groups, including Māori, consumers, clinicians, and services, so that development considers their perspectives and the operational realities of translating AI into clinical practice.
The AIGG is also planning a register of AI tools and communication with staff and the wider population on the governance process and the tools that have been reviewed.

unlisted_practices: Involve clinicians or clinical services from the beginning of AI concept and development.
Make AI outputs available within the patient's electronic health record.
Ensure key clinical decisions continue to be made by clinicians to preserve human oversight, judgement and evaluation.
Embed Māori data sovereignty principles and Māori partnership in AI governance, including Māori involvement in AI development.
Require AI developers to be transparent about training, testing and validation data, including how data were labelled.
Address protection of data if an AI company is sold and provisions for sharing IP and benefits in AI contracts.
Retain patient health data within the health service secure environment rather than sharing it with outside or commercial organisations.
Clearly define the problem and assess whether data are of sufficient scale and quality before deciding AI is appropriate.
Communicate publicly and transparently about projects using aggregated patient data.

screen.reason: This paper presents a framework and describes the establishment of a governance process for AI tools in health services in Aotearoa New Zealand, focusing on organizational recommendations and indigenous health equity rather than an empirical evaluation of an AI model.
